transcript.en: Every Monday, half our class arrives late. Our head teacher asked us why. We had a guess: maybe we are tired after the weekend. But a guess is not an answer. So we asked the data. Today: what data science is, and how you can use it. Data science means using data to answer a question. Data engineers collect and store the data. Data scientists ask it questions, find patterns, and explain what they mean. Data science is a loop with four steps. Ask a clear question. Collect the data you need. Explore it with numbers and charts. Then explain what you found, and ask the next question. Our teacher showed us the register, and we counted late arrivals for four weeks, day by day. Monday had twelve, the other days only about three. The pattern was clear, and it was not tiredness, because Friday was fine too. So we asked the next question: how do the late pupils travel? Most came on the same bus. On Mondays, it leaves the market late. The data led us to the real cause. A good data question is clear, you can measure it, and it is about something you can act on. Are pupils happy is hard to measure. How many pupils arrive late, on which days, is easy. Quick check! Which is the better data question for your class: do we like reading, or how many books did each of us borrow this term? Books borrowed this term. You can count it from the library cards, and compare classes. Liking reading matters too, but you would need a careful survey to measure it. In the app, open Tidy tables. A messy sheet gives the wrong answers. Fix it step by step, and watch the answers become right. Your turn. We explained our finding. What comes next in the loop? A new question. Remember: data science answers questions with data. Ask, collect, explore, explain, and go round again. Try it yourself: write three questions about your school that data could answer. Choose one, count the answer this week, and say where your number came from.

body.en:
Data is information we collect, like how many books each person in your class read this month. A data detective starts with a question, collects data to answer it, looks carefully at what they found, and then shares the answer.

A good question is one you can count or measure. “Do people like reading?” is hard to answer. “How many books did each pupil borrow this month?” is easy: you can count it from the library cards.

When you have your answer, it usually gives you a new question. If most books are borrowed on Mondays, you might ask: why Mondays? That is why data science is a loop, not a straight line.

البيانات معلومات نجمعها، مثل عدد الكتب التي قرأها كل شخص في فصلك هذا الشهر. ويبدأ محقّق البيانات بسؤال، ثم يجمع البيانات ليجيب عنه، وينظر بعناية فيما وجده، ثم يشارك الإجابة.

السؤال الجيد سؤال تستطيع أن تعدّه أو تقيسه. «هل يحب الناس القراءة؟» سؤال صعب الإجابة. أما «كم كتابًا استعار كل تلميذ هذا الشهر؟» فسهل: تستطيع عدّه من بطاقات المكتبة.

وحين تحصل على إجابتك، تعطيك عادةً سؤالًا جديدًا. فإذا استُعيرت معظم الكتب يوم الاثنين، فقد تسأل: لماذا الاثنين؟ ولهذا فعلم البيانات دورة، لا خط مستقيم.

transcript.en: A parent asked our teacher: how did the class do in the maths test? We had nine marks in front of us, without names. Nobody wants to hear all nine. We needed one fair number. Today: three kinds of middle, and how to measure the spread. The mean is what everyone would get if we shared the total equally. Add all the marks, then divide by how many there are. Our nine marks add to one hundred and sixteen, so the mean is about thirteen. The median is the middle mark when you line them up in order. With nine marks, it is the fifth one. Here, the median is thirteen. The mode is the mark that appears most often. Here, twelve and fourteen both appear twice, so there are two modes. The mode is handy for things you cannot add, like favourite colours. Now watch. One pupil was ill and scored zero. The mean drops to about eleven. The median only moves to twelve. One extreme mark pulls the mean, but hardly moves the median. A middle alone is not enough. Two classes can have the same mean, but one has marks from nine to sixteen, and the other from two to twenty. The range, highest minus lowest, shows the spread. Quick check! Most pupils get a little pocket money, but one gets a lot. Which middle describes a typical pupil best? The median. The one big amount pulls the mean up, so the mean looks richer than most pupils are. The median stays with the typical pupil. In the app, open The middle and the spread. Drag one pupil's mark from zero to twenty, and watch the mean, median, mode and range react. Your turn. A class has a range of eighteen marks. What does that tell you about the class? The marks are very spread out. Remember: the mean shares out, the median is the middle, the mode is the most common. And always give a spread with your middle. Try it yourself: ask ten friends how many minutes they walk to school. Work out the mean, the median and the range, and say which middle describes them best.

body.en:
There are three ways to find the “typical” value in a list of numbers. The mean: add them all up and divide by how many there are. The median: put them in order and take the one in the middle. The mode: the value that appears most often.

The range tells you how spread out the numbers are: the biggest minus the smallest.

Sometimes one number is much bigger than the others, like a friend who walks 60 minutes to school when everyone else walks about 10. That big number pulls the mean up, but the median stays in the middle, so the median often describes most people better.

transcript.en: Our class drew our town's rainfall as a pie chart. Twelve slices, one for each month. Nobody could see when the rains came. The data was right, but the chart was wrong. Today: which chart fits which question, and how charts can mislead. A bar chart compares groups. Which fruit does our class like best? One bar for each fruit, and the tallest bar wins. Mango wins easily here, with eleven pupils. A line chart shows change over time. Rainfall month by month makes a line that rises in the rainy season and falls again. Now everyone can see when the rains come. A pie chart shows how one whole is shared out, like the school budget: books, repairs, sports and food. Use it only with a few slices that add up to the whole. A scatter chart puts two measurements of each pupil on one picture, like hours of reading and spelling marks. Each dot is one pupil. If the dots rise together, the two go together. Now a trick to watch for. Our pass rate went from seventy to seventy four percent. If the axis starts at sixty eight, the new bar looks three times taller. Bars must start at zero. Quick check! You measured a bean plant every day for two weeks. Which chart shows how it grew? A line chart. The days go along the bottom, the height goes up, and the line shows the growth over time. You can even see the days when it grew fastest. In the app, open Pick the right chart. Match five questions to their charts, then drag where the axis starts and watch a small change look huge. Your turn. A poster shows two bars, and the axis starts at ninety. What should you check first? Where the axis starts. Remember: bars compare groups, lines show time, pies show parts of a whole, and scatter shows two measurements. And bars start at zero. Try it yourself: draw a bar chart of your family's favourite foods, with a title, labels and a scale from zero. Show it to someone and ask what they can tell from it.
transcript.ar: فصلنا رسم المطر في بلدنا رسمة دائرية. اتناشر حتة، حتة لكل شهر. محدش قدر يشوف المطر نزل إمتى. البيانات كانت صح، بس الرسمة كانت غلط. النهارده: أنهي رسمة تناسب أنهي سؤال، وإزاي الرسومات ممكن تضلّل. رسمة الأعمدة بتقارن بين مجموعات. فصلنا بيحب أنهي فاكهة أكتر؟ عمود لكل فاكهة، وأطول عمود هو الكسبان. المانجا كسبت بسهولة هنا، بحداشر تلميذ. رسمة الخطوط بتبيّن التغيّر مع الوقت. المطر شهر بشهر بيعمل خط بيطلع في موسم المطر وينزل تاني. دلوقتي الكل يقدر يشوف المطر بينزل إمتى. الرسمة الدائرية بتبيّن إزاي حاجة واحدة كاملة بتتقسم، زي ميزانية المدرسة: كتب وتصليحات ورياضة وأكل. استخدمها بس مع حتت قليلة مجموعها الكل. رسمة الانتشار بتحط قياسين لكل تلميذ في صورة واحدة، زي ساعات القراية ودرجات الإملا. كل نقطة تلميذ. لو النقط طالعة مع بعض، يبقى الاتنين ماشيين مع بعض. ودي خدعة لازم تاخد بالك منها. نسبة النجاح عندنا زادت من سبعين لأربعة وسبعين في المية. لو المحور بدأ من تمانية وستين، العمود الجديد يبان أطول تلات مرات. الأعمدة لازم تبدأ من الصفر. سؤال سريع! قستوا نبتة فول كل يوم لمدة أسبوعين. أنهي رسمة تبيّن إزاي كبرت؟ رسمة خطوط. الأيام تحت على المحور، والطول لفوق، والخط بيبيّن النمو مع الوقت. وتقدر كمان تشوف الأيام اللي كبرت فيها أسرع. في التطبيق، افتح «اختر الرسم المناسب». وصّل خمس أسئلة بالرسومات بتاعتها، وبعدين اسحب بداية المحور وشوف تغيير صغير بيبان ضخم إزاي. دورك. بوستر فيه عمودين، والمحور بيبدأ من تسعين. أول حاجة تتأكد منها إيه؟ المحور بيبدأ منين. افتكر: الأعمدة بتقارن مجموعات، والخطوط بتبيّن الوقت، والدائرة بتبيّن أجزاء من كل، والانتشار بيبيّن قياسين. والأعمدة بتبدأ من الصفر. جرّبها بنفسك: ارسم رسم بالأعمدة لأكلات عيلتك المفضلة، بعنوان وأسامي ومقياس بيبدأ من صفر. وورّيه لحد واسأله فهم منه إيه.

body.en:
A chart helps people see your data at a glance. A bar chart compares groups, like favourite fruits. A line chart shows how something changes over time, like the temperature each day. A pictogram uses small pictures, where each picture stands for a number.

Every good chart has a title, labels on both axes and units, such as “minutes” or “pupils”. The number scale on a bar chart should start at zero. If it starts higher, small differences look huge, and that is a trick.

Before you draw, ask: what question does my chart answer? Then choose the chart that answers it most clearly.
body.ar:
يساعد الرسم الناس على رؤية بياناتك بنظرة. الرسم بالأعمدة يقارن مجموعات، كالفواكه المفضّلة. والرسم الخطي يُظهر كيف يتغيّر شيء مع الوقت، كدرجة الحرارة كل يوم. والرسم بالصور يستعمل صورًا صغيرة، تمثّل كل صورة عددًا.

ولكل رسم جيد عنوان، وأسماء على المحورين، ووحدات مثل «دقائق» أو «تلاميذ». ويجب أن يبدأ مقياس الأرقام في الرسم بالأعمدة من الصفر. فإذا بدأ أعلى، بدت الفروق الصغيرة ضخمة، وهذه خدعة.

وقبل أن ترسم، اسأل: عن أيّ سؤال يجيب رسمي؟ ثم اختر الرسم الذي يجيب عنه بأوضح شكل.

transcript.en: A visitor told our school: the morning class does better than the afternoon class, so afternoon lessons should end. The averages agreed. But the averages were hiding something. Today: how to read data claims carefully, and how to keep pupils' data private. We looked inside the groups. The afternoon class had most of the pupils who joined this year, and many were still learning English. Within each group, the two classes scored about the same. So the time of day was not the cause. Two things can go together without one causing the other. Before you act on a pattern, ask: what else could explain it? Be careful with small groups too. A class of eight can swing a lot from one test to the next. One good or bad day changes the average. Look at several tests before you judge. Now privacy. When we share results, we share the class picture, not one person. Marks, health and family details stay private. A ranked list on the wall can hurt someone for years. Use pupil numbers instead of names. Collect only what your question needs. Keep the list of names locked away, and delete the data when you are done. Quick check! Pupils who eat breakfast at school get better marks. Does that prove breakfast causes better marks? Not on its own. Pupils who come early for breakfast may also miss fewer lessons, or live closer to school. Breakfast may well help, but the pattern alone does not prove it. A fair test would compare similar pupils. In the app, open the bias lab. See how data that leaves out a group gives unfair answers, and how fixing the data changes them. Your turn. Your class wants to show parents how it did in a test. What is the safest thing to share? The class average and spread, not names. Remember: look inside the groups, ask what else could explain a pattern, and be careful with small groups. Share the class, never the child. Try it yourself: find one claim with a number in an advert or a post. Ask what else could explain it, and what data would check it, before you share it.

body.en:
Adverts and posts often use numbers to convince you, like “9 out of 10 children love our juice!” A data detective asks three questions. How many people were asked? If it was only 10, that is not many. Who was asked? Maybe they were all at the juice company’s party. What else could explain it? Maybe the juice was free that day.

Data about people also needs care. Your marks, your health and where you live are private. When a class shares data, it should leave out names, and small groups are risky: if only one pupil walks from the village, everyone knows whose number it is.
